title: Three Ways a Signal Changes with Time

scenes.tts: The first film showed a cascade multiplying one input, then controlling its spread and shutoff. What can make an output fade, commit, or reset while input remains? One answer lies in how output loops back.
scenes.caption: The first film showed a cascade multiplying one input, then controlling its spread and shutoff. What can make an output fade, commit, or reset while input remains? One answer lies in how output loops back.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's 16:9 world and exact colour map: input GOLD; active relay BLUE; cGMP and error accumulator TEAL; open channels GREEN; shutoff and inhibitory feedback RED. Carry the same three-stage labelled-block cascade across the middle. A GOLD input stream enters from the left, BLUE activity reaches a large output gauge on the right, and faint arrows wait above and below the track. Keep a small 'schematic' label beside every curve and circuit cartoon. The input stream and gauge move continuously.
scenes.narration: The first film showed a cascade multiplying one input, then controlling its spread and shutoff. What can make an output fade, commit, or reset while input remains? One answer lies in how output loops back.

scenes.visual: Title 'Three Ways a Signal Changes with Time' fades in above the carried cascade. GOLD input continues entering and BLUE activity pulses toward the output gauge.

scenes.tts: Feedback begins when output changes its own production. A return arrow that reduces production is negative feedback. A return arrow that increases production is positive feedback.
scenes.caption: Feedback begins when output changes its own production. A return arrow that reduces production is negative feedback. A return arrow that increases production is positive feedback.
scenes.visual: The BLUE output gauge sends a curved arrow back to the middle relay. The arrow first becomes RED with a blunt inhibitory end and label 'negative'. It then transforms into a BLUE arrowhead with label 'positive'. The circuit remains the same size and keeps pulsing.
scenes.narration: Feedback begins when output changes its own production. A return arrow that reduces production is negative feedback. A return arrow that increases production is positive feedback.

scenes.tts: Timing and strength decide the result. The same pathway can therefore produce different dynamics. Connections alone cannot predict the time course.
scenes.caption: Timing and strength decide the result. The same pathway can therefore produce different dynamics. Connections alone cannot predict the time course.
scenes.visual: Carry the return arrow forward. A large clock and strength slider appear beside it. Moving either control morphs the BLUE output gauge between a brief pulse and a sustained level, both labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Timing and strength decide the result. The same pathway can therefore produce different dynamics. Connections alone cannot predict the time course.

scenes.tts: Start with a continuing input and a delayed brake. Output rises before the brake accumulates. Then negative feedback lowers pathway activity, even though input remains.
scenes.caption: Start with a continuing input and a delayed brake. Output rises before the brake accumulates. Then negative feedback lowers pathway activity, even though input remains.
scenes.visual: Keep the GOLD input bar high at the left. BLUE output fills the gauge quickly. RED brake blocks then accumulate one by one along the return arrow and press down the middle relay. The GOLD input remains visibly present.
scenes.narration: Start with a continuing input and a delayed brake. Output rises before the brake accumulates. Then negative feedback lowers pathway activity, even though input remains.

scenes.tts: The brake's delay and strength help shape the pulse. Connections alone did not predict it.
scenes.caption: The brake's delay and strength help shape the pulse. Connections alone did not predict it.
scenes.visual: Beside the carried circuit, draw a large schematic trace: BLUE output rises and falls while a GOLD input line stays high. Slide the RED brake's delay later and the pulse grows taller and wider; slide it earlier and the pulse shrinks. Label the trace 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The brake's delay and strength help shape the pulse. Connections alone did not predict it.

scenes.tts: Now turn the return arrow forward. Output strengthens its own production, so a small rise can recruit more activity.
scenes.caption: Now turn the return arrow forward. Output strengthens its own production, so a small rise can recruit more activity.
scenes.visual: Transform the RED brake arrow into a BLUE reinforcing arrow. Each pulse through the cascade sends another BLUE pulse backward, widening the next forward pulse. The output gauge rises more sharply with each pass.
scenes.narration: Now turn the return arrow forward. Output strengthens its own production, so a small rise can recruit more activity.

scenes.tts: If the loop is strong and includes a steep step, the circuit can settle into low or high output. A weaker loop may only sharpen the response.
scenes.caption: If the loop is strong and includes a steep step, the circuit can settle into low or high output. A weaker loop may only sharpen the response.
scenes.visual: At right, a shallow schematic landscape appears with a low basin and high basin. One output marker may settle in either basin; labels say 'low state' and 'high state', never 'only' or 'rejected'. Reduce the loop-strength slider and replace the landscape with one steeper schematic curve.
scenes.narration: If the loop is strong and includes a steep step, the circuit can settle into low or high output. A weaker loop may only sharpen the response.

scenes.tts: An ultrasensitive response is steep, but steepness alone can reverse when input falls. Sufficient positive feedback can add bistability and memory.
scenes.caption: An ultrasensitive response is steep, but steepness alone can reverse when input falls. Sufficient positive feedback can add bistability and memory.
scenes.visual: At left, a steep BLUE input-output curve appears with 'schematic' beneath it. A marker climbs and descends the same curve as GOLD input rises and falls. The reinforcing arrow then glows, and the low and high basins reappear conditionally.
scenes.narration: An ultrasensitive response is steep, but steepness alone can reverse when input falls. Sufficient positive feedback can add bistability and memory.

scenes.tts: Then a temporary input may leave output in the high state. The memory outlasts the input that set it.
scenes.caption: Then a temporary input may leave output in the high state. The memory outlasts the input that set it.
scenes.visual: In the schematic landscape, a brief GOLD push moves the output marker toward the high basin. After the push disappears, the marker remains there under the label 'with sufficient feedback'. The GOLD input line drops to zero while the marker stays high. Do not show single cells or a pooled bar.
scenes.narration: Then a temporary input may leave output in the high state. The memory outlasts the input that set it.

scenes.tts: A third circuit receives a continuing input. Three output traces appear on screen. Which trace represents adaptation? Look for the defining pattern before choosing.
scenes.caption: A third circuit receives a continuing input. Three output traces appear on screen. Which trace represents adaptation? Look for the defining pattern before choosing.
scenes.visual: Keep a GOLD input line high across the top. Below it, show three large unlabeled BLUE schematic traces: one stays high, one falls below its starting line, and one returns toward its starting line. Mark each plot 'schematic'. Place the question 'Which trace is adaptation?' above them. No circuit labels or answer appear.
scenes.narration: A third circuit receives a continuing input. Three output traces appear on screen. Which trace represents adaptation? Look for the defining pattern before choosing.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. The three traces and continuing GOLD input remain visible. A small cursor moves slowly among the traces without selecting one.

scenes.tts: Adaptation is the return toward rest while stimulus remains. So choose the trace returning toward its starting line. A delayed brake can make a similar shape. Integral feedback is a special negative feedback. It keeps correcting the gap from a reference output until the gap is zero.
scenes.caption: Adaptation is the return toward rest while stimulus remains. So choose the trace returning toward its starting line. A delayed brake can make a similar shape. Integral feedback is a special negative feedback. It keeps correcting the gap from a reference output until the gap is zero.
scenes.visual: Highlight the trace returning toward baseline and label it 'adaptation'. The other traces dim without crosses. Transform the selected plot into the carried pathway. Add a dashed TEAL reference line on the output gauge and a TEAL bracket showing the changing gap between current output and reference. The GOLD input remains visibly present.
scenes.narration: Adaptation is the return toward rest while stimulus remains. So choose the trace returning toward its starting line. A delayed brake can make a similar shape. Integral feedback is a special negative feedback. It keeps correcting the gap from a reference output until the gap is zero.

scenes.tts: In bacterial chemotaxis, receptor methylation acts as a running total of that gap in an idealized model. Correction continues until the error reaches zero. Engineers call this integral feedback. CheR adds methyl groups, while CheB removes them.
scenes.caption: In bacterial chemotaxis, receptor methylation acts as a running total of that gap in an idealized model. Correction continues until the error reaches zero. Engineers call this integral feedback. CheR adds methyl groups, while CheB removes them.
scenes.visual: Replace the generic relay with labelled blocks 'receptor', 'CheA', and 'CheY', all schematic and without molecular structures. A vertical TEAL ledger beside the receptor fills while output differs from the dashed reference. Small 'CheR adds' and 'CheB removes' tabs adjust a methylation gauge. The ledger stops changing as the output gauge returns to the reference.
scenes.narration: In bacterial chemotaxis, receptor methylation acts as a running total of that gap in an idealized model. Correction continues until the error reaches zero. Engineers call this integral feedback. CheR adds methyl groups, while CheB removes them.

scenes.tts: Changing enzyme amounts can change how quickly correction proceeds and can shift other steady behaviour. Yet adaptation precision can remain robust. Robustness protects a specified property, not every feature of the response.
scenes.caption: Changing enzyme amounts can change how quickly correction proceeds and can shift other steady behaviour. Yet adaptation precision can remain robust. Robustness protects a specified property, not every feature of the response.
scenes.visual: Duplicate the chemotaxis circuit into three rows with low, middle, and high schematic enzyme gauges. Their TEAL ledgers move at visibly different speeds. Each output approaches its own dashed pre-stimulus reference, while small timing clocks stop at different positions. Do not show identical absolute resting outputs across rows. A bracket labels only 'precision protected'.
scenes.narration: Changing enzyme amounts can change how quickly correction proceeds and can shift other steady behaviour. Yet adaptation precision can remain robust. Robustness protects a specified property, not every feature of the response.

scenes.tts: Place the three designs side by side. Delayed negative feedback can limit duration. Sufficient positive feedback can sharpen commitment and preserve memory. Integral feedback corrects until the error is zero. It can restore a reference output despite changing parts.
scenes.caption: Place the three designs side by side. Delayed negative feedback can limit duration. Sufficient positive feedback can sharpen commitment and preserve memory. Integral feedback corrects until the error is zero. It can restore a reference output despite changing parts.
scenes.visual: Arrange three versions of the same carried pathway across the frame. Left: RED delayed brake with a pulsed schematic trace. Middle: BLUE reinforcing loop with low and high state markers. Right: TEAL error ledger with return toward a dashed reference. GOLD input remains visible in all three. Each circuit pulses once when named.
scenes.narration: Place the three designs side by side. Delayed negative feedback can limit duration. Sufficient positive feedback can sharpen commitment and preserve memory. Integral feedback corrects until the error is zero. It can restore a reference output despite changing parts.

scenes.tts: The pathway's arrows begin the explanation, but kinetics finish it. Loop sign, strength, delay, and component lifetime determine whether output fades, commits, or adapts. Feedback reshapes time and reversibility.
scenes.caption: The pathway's arrows begin the explanation, but kinetics finish it. Loop sign, strength, delay, and component lifetime determine whether output fades, commits, or adapts. Feedback reshapes time and reversibility.
scenes.visual: Merge the three circuits back into one large pathway. Above it, four controls settle into place: 'sign', 'strength', 'delay', and 'lifetime'. Turning each control morphs the same BLUE schematic output trace among a pulse, a committed high state, and a return toward baseline. The moving pathway dims behind the end card.
scenes.narration: The pathway's arrows begin the explanation, but kinetics finish it. Loop sign, strength, delay, and component lifetime determine whether output fades, commits, or adapts. Feedback reshapes time and reversibility.

scenes.visual: Show one line only, centred over the dimmed moving circuit world: 'Feedback can limit duration, sharpen decisions, or restore resting output.' No title, subtitle, logo, or smaller line.
